name: Camera Follow
description:
Owns the view: where the world is drawn from, and the only transform applied to it. It follows a target within a deadzone rather than centring on it exactly, because a camera pinned to a walking character makes the whole world jitter under every step, and smooths what is left so a jump does not snap the view. It also composes screen shake into the same matrix, since a shake is a camera effect and two components cannot each own the transform — presentation.screen_shake publishes an offset and a roll, and yields the view when a camera is present. The target is read optionally rather than declared as a dependency, so the same camera follows a side-view body or a top-down walker without either being required.

AND IT CAN TURN, not just pan. A whole family of games keeps the body still in the middle of the screen and moves the WORLD around it — racing, skateboarding, biking, a dog on a lead, most sports where you are one player on a pitch. What makes those read correctly is that the view rotates with the thing it follows, so forward is always up the screen and a turn feels like the world swinging past rather than the player sliding sideways. That is a transform, and this component says it owns the only transform applied to the world, so it owns this one too — a second component composing its own rotation is exactly the collision the shake note above describes.

Rotation gets its own smoothing because it needs a different number from position. A camera that snaps to a heading is unreadable at speed and sickening at any speed, and the value that feels right for panning is far too quick for turning. Off by default: most games do not want it, and a view that rotates when nobody asked is worse than one that does not when they did.

inputs.name: deadzoneWidth
inputs.description: How far the target may move horizontally before the camera starts following, in world units. Zero pins the camera to the target and makes every footstep move the world.

inputs.name: deadzoneHeight
inputs.description: The vertical equivalent. Usually larger than it looks it should be: a jump is a big vertical excursion that the player does not want the camera to chase.

inputs.name: smoothingSeconds
inputs.description: Roughly how long the camera takes to close the gap once the target leaves the deadzone. 0 follows rigidly; large values read as the camera losing track.

inputs.name: clampToWorldBounds
inputs.description: Whether the view is kept inside the world rectangle, so the edge of the level is never on screen. Turn it off for a world with no meaningful edge.

inputs.name: zoom
inputs.description: Scale applied to the view. Above 1 shows less of the world and makes the camera's work visible even in a level that would otherwise fit on one screen.

inputs.name: followRotation
inputs.description: Whether the view turns with the target's facing, so forward is always up the screen and the world moves around a body that stays put. Needs a target that HAS a facing — movement.vehicle_basic under `continuous` motion publishes one; a stepped vehicle does not, and the camera stays upright rather than inventing a heading.

inputs.name: rotationSmoothingSeconds
inputs.description: Roughly how long the view takes to catch up to a new heading. Separate from smoothingSeconds because the right answer differs: a camera that snaps to heading is unreadable at speed, and panning wants a much quicker number than turning. 0 snaps.

outputs.name: center
outputs.description: The point the view is centred on, in world units.

outputs.name: ownsViewTransform
outputs.description: Always true while this component is in the build. Anything that would otherwise set its own view transform reads this and yields, so the view has exactly one owner.

outputs.name: rotation
outputs.description: The view's current angle in radians, after smoothing. 0 whenever followRotation is off, so a consumer can compose it unconditionally.

outputs.name: view
outputs.description: The view transform this component set on the canvas this frame, as a 2D affine matrix {a,b,c,d,e,f} taking world pixels to screen pixels. Published so a host can invert it -- a pointer lands on the screen, and the tile under it is on the other side of this matrix. Identity until the first draw.
